key_terms.meaning: Steady voltage across a cell membrane at rest, about −70 mV inside relative to outside, set mainly by K⁺ leak and the Na⁺/K⁺ pump
Brief all-or-none reversal of membrane voltage to about +30 mV, then back, lasting 1–2 ms in nerve
The depolarisation level (about −55 mV) a stimulus must reach before an action potential fires
E = (RT/zF)·ln([ion]out/[ion]in), the equilibrium voltage for one ion species across the membrane
Fixed DC voltage an electrode metal develops against body electrolyte; differs between metals and adds an offset to the bio-signal
Charged layer of ions in the electrolyte that sits against the electrode surface and lets ionic current cross into electronic current
Complex opposition (resistance plus capacitance) at the electrode–skin interface, typically 1–10 kΩ for a good surface electrode
Electrode with a tip of 1 µm or less, used to record from a single cell without damaging it
Device that converts one form of energy (force, pressure, temperature, light) into an electrical output
Resistive element whose resistance changes with stretch; gauge factor G = (ΔR/R)/(ΔL/L)
Four-arm resistive network that converts a small resistance change into a measurable voltage; output V₀ = V·(ΔR/R)/4 for one active arm
Production of charge across certain crystals when stressed, used for pressure and vibration sensors
Three-op-amp difference amplifier with very high input impedance and high gain, the front end of every bio-amplifier
Common-mode rejection ratio, CMRR = 20·log₁₀(A_d/A_cm) in dB; tells how well the amplifier rejects the shared interference voltage
Model of the heart as a dipole viewed by leads I, II and III on the two arms and left leg, with lead II = lead I + lead III
NCV = d / (t₂ − t₁), where d is the distance between two stimulation points in metres and t₂ − t₁ is the difference in latency in seconds
Portable recorder that stores a continuous 24-hour ECG on the patient for later scanning and arrhythmia analysis
Small EEG response time-locked to a repeated stimulus (visual, auditory or somatosensory), recovered by averaging many trials
Training method in which a patient sees or hears a filtered EEG or EMG signal and learns to change it
Pressure-sensitive platform or insole that maps foot loading during standing and walking

takeaways: Every bioelectric signal starts as an ion movement across a membrane, so the source voltage is always a chemical battery of a few tens of millivolts.
An electrode is an ionic-to-electronic converter; its half-cell potential and its impedance decide how clean the recorded signal will be.
A transducer must be chosen by range, sensitivity, linearity, impedance and safety for the specific body variable, not by one single best type.
A bio-amplifier's job is to multiply the difference between two electrodes and throw away the interference both share, which is why CMRR and input impedance matter more than plain gain.
The ECG recorder is a calibrated voltmeter and clock: standard leads, 1 mV calibration pulse, 25 mm/s paper speed and 10 mm/mV sensitivity.
EEG needs microvolt gain in a 0.5–70 Hz band while EMG needs millivolt gain up to about 500 Hz; one amplifier setting cannot serve both.
Nerve conduction velocity turns two latency readings at two stimulation sites into a number in metres per second that separates normal nerve from demyelination.
Most ECG faults are found by checking, in order, the patient, the electrode, the cable and amplifier, and lastly the mains interference path.
Averaging and filtering pull evoked potentials out of background EEG because the response repeats while the noise does not.
Biofeedback works only when the measured signal is clean and the feedback reaches the patient within a fraction of a second.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit are almost always asked as a signal path — physiology, then electrode, then amplifier, then recorder or display — so draw the block chain and give a number with units at every block.

bank.q: Explain the origin of the resting membrane potential and the action potential in a nerve cell, and state typical voltage and time values.
outline: Ion concentrations inside and outside the cell with typical millivolt values
K⁺ leak sets the resting voltage near −70 mV; Na⁺/K⁺ pump maintains gradients
Nernst and Goldman relations used to compute equilibrium voltages
Depolarisation to threshold near −55 mV opens voltage-gated Na⁺ channels
Peak near +30 mV, repolarisation by K⁺ efflux, refractory period
All-or-none law and propagation along the axon

bank.q: Describe the electrode–electrolyte interface, half-cell potential and why electrode impedance must match the amplifier.
outline: Ionic current in tissue, electronic current in wire, conversion at the interface
Double layer model and its capacitance
Half-cell potential; offset from two different metals; need for Ag/AgCl pairs
Polarisation, non-polarisable electrodes, electrode jelly and skin preparation
Typical surface electrode impedance 1–10 kΩ; causes of drift and motion artefact
Why amplifier input impedance must be many times the electrode impedance

bank.q: Compare surface, needle and microelectrodes with respect to size, impedance, signal amplitude and clinical use.
outline: Surface: large area, high impedance, invasive-free, used for ECG and EEG
Needle: penetrates skin, low impedance, used for EMG and fetal ECG
Microelectrode: tip 1 µm or less, used for intracellular recording
Table of size, impedance, bandwidth and typical signal range
Sterilisation, safety and disposable versus reusable practice

bank.q: List the criteria for selecting a physiological transducer and apply them to a blood-pressure sensor and a foot-pressure sensor.
outline: Range, sensitivity, linearity, hysteresis, resolution, bandwidth
Impedance matching, excitation requirement, output type
Biocompatibility, sterilisation, size, weight, safety, cost
Resistive strain-gauge type for blood pressure via diaphragm
Piezoelectric or resistive pressure pad for pedobarograph
Reasoned comparison against capacitive and inductive alternatives

bank.q: Draw and explain the block diagram of an ECG recording system and describe the normal ECG waves with their amplitudes and durations.
outline: Electrodes, lead selector, protection circuit, instrumentation amplifier, filters, isolation, ADC or pen drive
Calibration pulse 1 mV, paper speed 25 mm/s, sensitivity 10 mm/mV
P wave, PR interval, QRS complex, ST segment, T wave with typical values
Einthoven leads I, II, III and augmented leads; standard 12-lead layout
Why isolation and patient leakage-current limits are mandatory

bank.q: A bio-amplifier must handle a 1 mV differential ECG signal sitting on a 300 mV common-mode interference. Explain how an instrumentation amplifier solves this and calculate the CMRR needed if the interference at the output must stay at or below 0.1% of the signal.
outline: Differential gain A_d and common-mode gain A_cm defined
Instrumentation amplifier built from three op-amps; input buffers give very high impedance
CMRR = 20 log₁₀(A_d/A_cm)
Target interference-to-signal ratio 10⁻³ at output means A_d/A_cm must be at least 1000
CMRR ≈ 60 dB minimum, so a practical design targets 80–100 dB
Shielded cable, driven right leg and notch filter as supporting measures

bank.q: A load cell has four strain gauges of 350 Ω and gauge factor 2.0, all four active in a Wheatstone bridge fed with 5 V. Strain is 1000 µε. Compute the output voltage and explain how this becomes a patient weight.
outline: Gauge factor definition G = (ΔR/R)/(ΔL/L)
Fractional resistance change = 2.0 × 1000 × 10⁻⁶ = 2 × 10⁻³
All-four-active bridge output ≈ V × (ΔR/R), giving about 10 mV
Amplify to a few volts, digitise with the ADC
Calibration with known weights; zeroing before each use
Load cell used in weighing scales and in gait platforms

bank.q: In a nerve conduction study the median nerve is stimulated at the wrist and at the elbow. Latency is 3.5 ms at the wrist and 7.5 ms at the elbow, and the separation is 240 mm. Calculate the conduction velocity and state how the result is interpreted.
outline: Latency difference = 7.5 − 3.5 = 4.0 ms, which removes the distal motor delay
Distance = 0.24 m
Compare with normal range for the nerve, typically about 50–65 m/s in the arm
Slowing suggests demyelination; small amplitude suggests axonal loss
Temperature and limb position affect the value

bank.q: Design the recording chain for an EMG channel and for an EEG channel, stating gain, bandwidth, filter and sampling rate for each, and justify the differences.
outline: EEG amplitude 10–100 µV, band 0.5–70 Hz, gain of order 10⁴–10⁵
EMG amplitude 0.1–5 mV, band 10–500 Hz, gain of order 10²–10³
High-pass removes electrode drift; low-pass suppresses muscle noise in EEG
Notch at 50 Hz for mains interference
Sampling at least twice the highest frequency: 200 Hz for EEG, 1–2 kHz for EMG
Common-mode rejection and input impedance requirements common to both

bank.q: Explain how a heart-rate monitor detects beats, and how a Holter monitor differs from it in recording, leads and analysis.
outline: QRS detection by amplitude threshold or slope/derivative algorithm
Beat-to-beat interval, averaging over 8–10 beats, bradycardia and tachycardia alarms
Artefact rejection: T waves, muscle noise, motion
Holter: 2–3 modified chest leads, 24 hours, solid-state memory
Scanning for ST episodes, arrhythmias, heart-rate variability, patient diary
Maintenance points for both: battery, electrodes, calibration

bank.q: An ECG recording shows a thick 50 Hz baseline. Separate the possible faults into patient, electrode, amplifier and interference categories, and give the check and the cure for each.
outline: Patient: movement, sweating, shivering — rest and reassure
Electrode: dry or loose, old jelly, high impedance, wrong half-cell metal — clean skin, new Ag/AgCl electrodes
Amplifier: gain, filter, calibration and lead-off settings — check calibration pulse
Interference: broken shield, ungrounded bed, mains and diathermy nearby — use driven right leg, notch filter, shielded cable
Wandering baseline from respiration and electrode drift
Decide by substitution: swap cable, swap electrodes, use simulator

bank.q: Discuss multichannel EEG recording in epilepsy, the use of evoked potentials, and the place of MEG as a complementary method.
outline: Electrode placement by the 10–20 system; 19 or 21 channels; montages
Epilepsy: interictal spikes and slow waves, focus localisation, activation procedures
Averaging for visual, auditory and somatosensory evoked potentials, 100–1000 trials
Latency and amplitude of the recovered waveform used in diagnosis
MEG measures the magnetic field of the same currents; needs shielding and SQUID sensors
Evaluate: EEG gives good temporal but poor spatial resolution; MEG better spatial, higher cost; combinations are complementary

bank.q: Describe the instrumentation for EEG and EMG biofeedback and evaluate the factors that decide whether such training can succeed.
outline: Electrodes, high-gain low-noise amplifier, band-pass filter for the chosen band
Rectify and integrate, or count events, to get one slowly varying number
Feedback within a fraction of a second; visual bar or audio tone with threshold
Baseline session, threshold raised gradually, number of sessions
Evaluate: signal quality, latency, patient motivation, artefact from eye blinks and jaw clonus
Uses: relaxation training, re-education of pelvic-floor and wrist muscles

bank.q: For a gait laboratory, choose sensors for foot pressure, joint angle, velocity and acceleration, and explain how the numbers are combined to describe a walking cycle.
outline: Pedobarograph platform or insole for plantar pressure mapping
Potentiometer, goniometer or IMU for limb position and joint angle
Accelerometer and gyroscope for acceleration and angular velocity
Velocity from integration of acceleration or from timing markers
Walking cycle: heel strike, loading, stance, toe-off, swing
Evaluate: cable tangle versus wireless IMU, calibration, drift and repeatability

glossary.def: Voltage produced by living tissue, such as the membrane voltage of a nerve or muscle cell or the body-surface copy of many such cells.
Loss of the negative resting voltage as positive ions enter the cell.
Return of the membrane voltage to its resting negative value after an action potential.
Short time after an action potential when the cell cannot fire again, which limits the maximum firing rate.
Active transport that pushes Na⁺ out and K⁺ in to keep the concentration gradients that make the resting potential.
Silver wire coated with silver chloride, used as a stable, low-offset, non-polarisable biopotential electrode.
Build-up of charge at an electrode that opposes current flow and distorts low-frequency signals.
False signal caused by movement of the electrode on the skin, which changes the half-cell potential.
Electrode pair that records the difference between two nearby active sites.
Active electrode referred to one distant common reference, so the signal contains more of the remote activity.
Electrode placed over the source of interest; the other is the reference or indifferent electrode.
Ratio of fractional resistance change to fractional length change in a strain gauge, about 2 for metal foil.
Force transducer made of a metal element with bonded strain gauges wired as a Wheatstone bridge.
Sensor that converts displacement or pressure into a change of capacitance.
Sensor that converts displacement into a change of inductance, for example by moving a core in a coil.
Sensor that converts light intensity into current or voltage, used for pulse and blood-oxygen measurement.
Circuit that passes the signal across an optical or transformer barrier so no mains fault current can reach the patient.
Narrow band-stop filter, usually set at 50 Hz in India, that removes mains interference with little loss elsewhere.
Analogue-to-digital converter; its resolution in bits and its sampling rate set the quality of the stored signal.
False low-frequency signal created when the sampling rate is below twice the highest signal frequency.
Time from a stimulus to the start of the evoked or muscle response, measured in milliseconds.
Fall in the median frequency and rise in amplitude of the EMG spectrum as a muscle is held contracted.
Standard spacing of EEG electrodes by percentages of the skull landmarks, giving named positions such as Fz, C3 and O2.
Superconducting quantum interference device, the extremely sensitive magnetic sensor used in MEG.
